strengths: The paper conducts extensive experiments across nine datasets and three tasks (object classification, action recognition, and human pose estimation), showing competitive or state-of-the-art accuracy while being lightweight.

The proposed Event Cloud representation preserves polarity and chronological order, avoiding the preprocessing cost of frame/voxel transformations; Table 3 reports lower preprocessing time than several baselines.

The frequency-domain modules aim to reduce Multiply Accumulate Operations (MACs) and handle long event sequences; Table 5 shows a very low MACs count and high throughput compared with frame-based and voxel-based methods.
The ablation study supports the roles of event-based grouping/sampling, temporal frequency extraction, and polarity on three datasets.
weaknesses: The core 'Spatial-FA' module applies the Fourier transform along the feature/channel dimension rather than the spatial (x,y) dimensions. Calling it spatial-frequency analysis is misleading, and the paper does not justify that channel-wise FFT captures explicit spatial structure.

The Event Cloud representation is not clearly differentiated from prior event-cloud or point-based event representations; the main innovations (D-FPS, EF-KNN, CES, frequency filtering) are incremental combinations of existing point-cloud and GFNet-style ideas.

The experimental evaluation lacks error bars, repeated runs, or statistical significance tests. Many reported improvements over strong baselines are small (e.g., Table 2, Table 4), and the single large UCF101-DVS gain is not sufficiently analyzed.

Several datasets use a random 20% test split (e.g., UCF101-DVS, CIFAR10-DVS, ASL-DVS, Daily DVS) while using sliding windows, which can cause train/test leakage from the same video sequences and may inflate the reported action recognition results.

Reproducibility is weak: the code link appears blank, and key details are missing, including the downsampling procedure for Event Cloud, the scaling factor alpha in D-FPS, FFT filter initialization, K/group-size selections, and how FFT/Hadamard operations are counted in MACs.

Presentation has multiple issues: typos ('Abaltion', 'Tansformer', 'ALS-DVS'), ambiguous table headers (duplicate MPJPE_AD columns), unclear definitions (e.g., Std in Eq. 8), and inconsistent claims such as 'raw unprocessed Event Cloud' despite downsampling and normalization.
No limitations section or ethical statement is included, and efficiency claims are not fully supported by accounting for FFT overhead, complex arithmetic, or end-to-end latency on different hardware.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: efficient event-based vision without costly frame/voxel conversion, and it evaluates a unified model on nine datasets across classification, action recognition, and pose estimation.
The Event Cloud representation has practical appeal: it preserves polarity and raw temporal ordering and requires only downsampling, as shown in the preprocessing-time comparison.
The idea of using frequency-domain global filters for long event sequences is plausible for capturing long-range temporal dependencies and reducing some computation.
The hardware benchmark and ablation attempt to quantify efficiency and the roles of polarity/temporal modules, and the DHP19 pose results are relatively strong.
The architecture is described with a pipeline algorithm and diagrams, making the high-level design easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification for Spatial-FA is unsound or at least very unclear. The paper invokes the convolution theorem, but the module applies DFT over feature/channel dimensions rather than over spatial (x,y) or temporal coordinates. A Hadamard product over channel-frequency coefficients is not mathematically equivalent to the spatial/temporal convolution being replaced, so the claimed efficiency-accuracy equivalence and the 'spatial frequency' interpretation are not supported.

Novelty is overstated. Event Cloud/space-time event clouds were already used in prior work (e.g., Wang et al., WACV 2019 [48]), and the proposed representation is essentially point cloud plus polarity and temporal ordering. D-FPS/EF-KNN/CES are incremental modifications of PointNet++-style grouping/sampling, and the frequency modules closely follow existing frequency-domain networks (FFC, GFNet).

Experimental evidence is inconsistent and not reproducible enough. Table 2 reports N-Caltech101 accuracy 0.824 for FECNet, while Table 8 reports values around 60 for the same dataset (apparently under a different 300 ms window) without explaining the metric, protocol, or window aggregation. The huge UCF101-DVS gain (0.916 vs 0.787/0.725) likewise lacks protocol details and repeated runs, and no standard deviations are reported.

Reproducibility is weak. The code URL is missing in the manuscript, and key details are omitted: initialization/constraints for the learnable frequency filter V (especially conjugate symmetry for real outputs), alpha values for D-FPS, K in EF-KNN, definition of Std(.,.) in Eq. 8, how F_C is expanded for concatenation in Eq. 9, how windows are aggregated, and exact training/validation splits for 'random 20%' datasets.

Method presentation has multiple errors and ambiguities. The inverse DFT in Eq. 11 uses sigma instead of pi in the exponent, Eq. 8's Std takes two arguments, dimensions after Eqs. 6-9 are unclear, and Eq. 12 applies a nonlinear activation after iFFT without specifying whether complex outputs are handled. The algorithm also omits most hyperparameters.

The ablation study does not isolate the core contributions convincingly. Removing Temporal-FA changes UCF101-DVS only from 0.916 to 0.913 and N-CARS from 0.947 to 0.944; removing polarity gives similarly small changes. There is no ablation removing Spatial-FA or replacing it with a standard convolutional/MLP block, so the value of the frequency modules is not demonstrated.

Efficiency claims are incomplete or misleading. The 'one-thousandth of MACs' statement does not match Table 5 ratios (e.g., 0.109G vs 59.28G is about 1/544), the '20x' and '60x' complexity reductions are not reconciled, and FPS/KNN/grouping costs are not included in MACs or reported preprocessing/inference cost. The claim about 'tensor decomposition technique employed' in FECNet is not described in the method and appears inaccurate.

Presentation quality is below standard: typos ('Abaltion', 'moule', 'ALS-DVS'), missing metric labels in Table 8, unexplained window choices (30 ms for N-Caltech101 in Table 1 vs 300 ms in Table 8), and unclear definitions reduce confidence in the reported results.

Significance is limited by missing comparisons to recent event-cloud/point-based methods (e.g., EventMamba, which is cited but not compared) and by the fact that most gains over TTPOINT/SpikePoint are small or inconsistent. The paper's broad SOTA claims are not adequately supported by the evidence presented.

strengths: Targets an important problem: efficient event-based vision without expensive frame/voxel conversion, while preserving polarity and fine-grained temporal information.
Provides a broad empirical evaluation across nine datasets and three task families (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), including efficiency benchmarks and ablations.

The proposed Event Cloud representation that treats (x,y,t,p) differently from standard point clouds is conceptually sensible, and the ablation without polarity, although modest, supports the intuition that polarity can add information.

The reported efficiency numbers are striking: FECNet achieves 0.898M parameters, 0.109G MACs, and 229.7 FPS on DVS128 Gesture, and it outperforms several frame/voxel/point-based methods on action recognition and pose estimation benchmarks.
The preprocessing-time comparison in Table 3 supports the claim that Event Cloud downsampling can be much cheaper than constructing frames, voxels, or binary maps.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central frequency-domain justification is unclear and potentially incorrect. The convolution theorem applies to convolution along the dimension being transformed, but the Spatial-FA module appears to apply FFT along the channel/feature dimension (complexity O((2D+4) log(2D+4)) vs O((2D+4)^2)). Replacing a channel-wise linear operation with a global frequency filter is not theoretically equivalent to spatial/temporal convolution as claimed, so the main source of both efficiency and feature extraction is not adequately justified.

Soundness: The Temporal-FA module assumes a meaningful temporal ordering over the T/2 centroids, but those centroids are produced by D-FPS and updated by mean coordinates. Farthest-point sampling returns points in distance-based order, not chronological order, so applying a FFT over this dimension may not model the true event sequence. The paper does not clarify whether chronological order is preserved or why the temporal Fourier transform remains valid after grouping and coordinate evolution.

Soundness: The Event-based Grouping & Sampling module is underspecified. It is unclear whether alpha is learnable or fixed, how K is chosen, how EF-KNN distances behave in high-dimensional feature space, and how the standardization and concatenation equations map dimensions, especially the broadcasting of centroids' features F_C. The ablations show only small gains for the proposed G&S over a point-based version (e.g., 0.937 vs 0.947 on N-CARS, 6.27 vs 6.11 on DHP19), so the strong claims about faithfully extracting 2S-1T-1P structure are not fully supported.

Soundness/Evaluation: Several comparisons are not clearly controlled. UCF101-DVS shows a very large gain over prior SOTA, but the input event number, sliding-window protocol, train/test split, parameter count, and MACs are not matched to all baselines. Since Table 8 shows performance depends strongly on event number, FECNet's advantage may partly reflect using more events rather than a fundamentally better representation.

Reproducibility: The code link is missing from the abstract, and key training details are omitted or vague: batch size is 'dynamically set to take full use of the GPU's memory', no random seeds are reported, no standard deviations or repeated runs are given, and several datasets use a random 20% test split without fixed seed or split listing. This makes it difficult to reproduce or compare results reliably.

Evidence: Ablations are limited and lack error bars. There is no ablation of Spatial-FA alone, despite it being a core claimed contribution. The ablation table also uses 'w/o TFT' while the method section describes Temporal-FA (TFA), which is confusing. Claims of robustness and efficiency would be stronger with controlled module removal and variance estimates.

Presentation: The manuscript contains multiple typos and ambiguities ('moulde', 'Bina-Rep', 'TFT' vs 'TFA', inconsistent acronyms, unexplained notation), and the tables often lack standard deviations or sample sizes. The distinction between Event Cloud and point cloud is more semantic than technical if point-based methods can also include (x,y,t,p), so the novelty needs sharper positioning.

Limitations/Ethics: The paper does not discuss limitations, failure cases, energy cost, or ethical considerations, despite motivating the work by low-power event cameras. The low-MAC claim is also not accompanied by measured energy or end-to-end latency beyond a single FPS benchmark.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant bottleneck in event-based vision: frame/voxel representations require costly transformations and lose fine-grained temporal information. Using Event Cloud representation with minimal preprocessing is a meaningful direction.

The empirical coverage is broad: ten datasets across object classification, action recognition, and human pose estimation, with reported strong results in several settings (e.g., UCF101-DVS 0.916, THU E-ACT-50 97.25, DHP19 MPJPE2D/3D 6.11/69.89).

The model is lightweight in reported parameter and GMAC counts (Tables 6, 7, 12), and the FPGA comparison, if valid, suggests potential efficiency advantages over MLP-based spatial feature extraction.

The Event-based Grouping and Sampling design attempts to treat spatial, temporal, and polarity dimensions differently, which is a sensible departure from simply treating events as standard point clouds.
The ablation studies on module variants and event number scalability provide some evidence that the temporal-frequency and grouping components contribute, though the evidence is incomplete.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient for ICML: the code link is blank, random seeds and variance are not reported, and key implementation details (complex FFT handling, filter parameterization, training schedules, dataset splits for non-official partitions) are missing.

Several mathematical and architectural descriptions are inconsistent or incorrect. Equation 12 defines a standardization operation in an ambiguous/nonstandard way; D-FPS scales polarity by a learnable factor without justification; EF-KNN uses feature-space distances while coordinate evolution uses grouped coordinates, leaving the grouping semantics unclear.

The frequency-domain replacement for MLP is not theoretically justified. Hadamard multiplication in the Fourier domain corresponds to circular convolution with a global filter, not to an arbitrary MLP; the paper provides no expressiveness analysis or discussion of padding, real/complex operations, or boundary effects.

The hardware benchmark in Table 10 is not credible as presented: SFA cycle count is exactly constant (393,859) across different FFT lengths and input dimensions, and on-chip memory accounting is opaque. No synthesis setup, dataflow, bitwidth, or measurement methodology is provided, making the claimed 16x-64x speedups unreproducible.

Scalability claims are weakened by the paper's own Table 12: runtime and GMACs grow superlinearly with event number and centroid count, and the method still fixes sampled event counts and grouping sizes. Scaling to arbitrary high-resolution or long-sequence events without retraining is not demonstrated.

Experimental comparisons are not controlled: baselines differ in representation, event count, pretraining, and data splits. On UCF101-DVS the improvement over the strong point-based EventMamba baseline is only about 1.3 percentage points, so the claim of a 16% improvement needs clearer definition and stronger support.

Presentation quality is poor: typos and inconsistencies (ALS-DVS vs. ASL-DVS, THU E-ACT-50, missing averages), undefined symbols in Algorithm 1, malformed table dimensions in Table 13, and missing entries in Table 1 reduce confidence in the reported numbers.

The originality is incremental: Event Cloud representation and frequency-domain feature extraction are both existing ideas, and the paper does not sufficiently separate the benefit of structural polarity integration from these existing components.

There is no dedicated limitations section, failure-case analysis, or meaningful ethical discussion. The impact statement is generic and does not address potential misuse, bias, or computational resource concerns.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: ten datasets and three task families (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), with ablations on modules (Table 8), event-number scalability (Table 9), and an FPGA study of the frequency module vs a spatial MLP (Table 10), providing more evaluation than is typical in this space.

Efficiency motivation is well-targeted: Event Cloud requires the least preprocessing time (Table 4), and SECNet is genuinely small (e.g., 1.126M params / 0.48 GMACs in Table 6; 1.83M / 0.160 GMACs on DHP19 in Table 7), which is a relevant property for edge event-camera deployment.

Some results are competitive or strong, particularly action recognition: 0.916 on UCF101-DVS vs 0.903 for the recent EventMamba (Table 3) and 97.25% on THU E-ACT-50 (Table 5), with a clear scalability trend as event count grows (Table 9).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited and overstated. Spatial-FA/Temporal-FA are essentially GFNet-style learnable global filters applied via FFT/Hadamard/iFFT (Eq. 15), and the paper does not articulate what is new beyond reapplication to Event Cloud. The 'structural polarity integration' reduces to a learnable 4-dim scaling factor alpha in D-FPS plus feature-based KNN; the corresponding ablation shows only marginal or mixed effects (w/o alpha: 6.11->6.17 / 69.89->70.03 on DHP19; structural polarity is actually worse than input-level polarity on NCARS, 0.937 vs 0.944), so the headline contribution of embedding polarity 'structurally' is not convincingly supported.

Central claims of superiority are not supported by the evidence. Object-classification average is 0.905 vs 0.902 for VMST-Net (Table 2), i.e., within noise, yet the paper repeatedly frames SECNet as dominant/'ground-breaking.' Critically, the internal ablation in Table 13 shows SECNet underperforms its own CNN variant (ECNet) on several datasets (UCF101-DVS 0.916 vs 0.941; N-CARS 0.947 vs 0.951), meaning the frequency module is a compute-for-accuracy trade rather than a demonstrated accuracy win, which is not reconciled with the abstract's effectiveness claims.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence: UCF101-DVS GMACs are reported as 0.48 in Table 6 but 0.345 in Table 13 with no explanation of differing configurations; FPS is 120 in Table 6 while the appendix states 229.7 FPS; Table 13's header and per-row metric alignment are garbled, making the reported values hard to attribute to the correct metric/dataset.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the abstract ends with 'Our code will be available at:' and no URL, no variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are given despite several claims resting on <1% margins, and several datasets use a non-standard random 20% test split (Section D), complicating comparison with published numbers.

Presentation and care are below bar for a top venue: the reference list contains a leftover template placeholder ('Langley... Crafting papers on machine learning... ICML 2000'), multiple citation years do not match the bibliography (e.g., Lichtsteiner et al., 2023 vs 2008; Chen et al., 2022b attached to a 2024 super-resolution paper), and there are pervasive typos and mislabeled tables, which raises broader concerns about rigor.

The scalability claim is only partially demonstrated: super-linear growth of MACs with points/groups is acknowledged (Appendix E, Table 12), so the method does not fully escape the limitation it criticizes in point-based methods, and no head-to-head accuracy comparison at matched compute is provided to show TFA justifies replacing LSTM/attention.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in event-based vision: expensive frame/voxel preprocessing and loss of fine-grained temporal information. Event Cloud representation and the SECNet pipeline provide a useful alternative; Table 4 shows much lower preprocessing time (e.g., 1.5 ms vs. 14.6 ms for voxel grid on N-Caltech101).

The frequency-domain modules are a sensible efficiency-oriented design. The paper gives complexity arguments for Spatial-FA versus MLP and supports them with hardware measurements: Table 10 reports 393,859 cycles for SFA across stages versus 6.3M/12.6M/25.2M cycles for MLP, with lower on-chip memory.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: ten datasets across object classification, action recognition, and human pose estimation, with ablations, scalability studies, runtime tables, and visualizations. Results are strong on action recognition, e.g., UCF101-DVS 0.916 vs. EventMamba 0.903 and VMST-Net 0.787; THU E-ACT-50 97.25 vs. EV-ACT 92.7.

The proposed Event-based G&S module makes a reasonable attempt to handle spatial, temporal, and polarity dimensions differently via D-FPS, EF-KNN, and CES. Ablations in Table 8 show that removing these components generally degrades performance.

SECNet is lightweight and scalable in practice: Table 7 reports 1.831M parameters and 0.160 GMACs for DHP19 versus 3.65M/5.03 for Point Transformer, while Table 9 shows improving accuracy with larger event counts.
The paper includes practical hardware analysis, pseudo-code, runtime lookup tables, and an impact statement, which improve its usefulness for edge-oriented event-based perception.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate. Event Cloud representation was introduced previously, and frequency-domain global filters are well established in vision (e.g., GFNet/FFC). The main contribution is an effective combination and engineering of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new principle for event-based learning.

The frequency-domain modeling is not fully justified for event streams. TFA applies a DFT along the event index dimension rather than the actual event timestamps, even though event distributions are highly non-uniform in time. It is not shown that this captures physically meaningful temporal structure rather than index-order artifacts. Similarly, Spatial-FA applies a DFT over the feature/channel dimension, which assumes ordered channel semantics that are not guaranteed.

The claim that polarity is integrated structurally is only weakly supported. Table 8 shows very small differences between full SECNet and variants without polarity or with input-level polarity (e.g., N-CARS 0.947 vs. 0.944, UCF101-DVS 0.916 vs. 0.913), and in some cases the no-polarity variant is competitive. The structural benefit of polarity is therefore not convincingly isolated.

Reproducibility and statistical rigor are incomplete. No code or seed information is available, several datasets use random 20% test splits, batch size is dynamically chosen, and no error bars or repeated-run variance are reported. Object classification gains are often marginal (e.g., N-Caltech101 0.824 vs. 0.822, CIFAR10-DVS 0.757 vs. 0.753, N-CARS 0.947 vs. 0.944), so significance is unclear.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Methods differ in representation, pretraining, splitting protocol, event-number settings, and hardware; some numbers are taken from prior papers rather than re-evaluated under a unified protocol. This weakens the strength of the SOTA claims, especially on object classification.

Presentation has issues that hinder assessment: Figure 3 is overcrowded, reference entries contain duplicates/mismatches (e.g., ECSNet and Chen et al. citations), and Table 13 in the appendix is difficult to parse. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations or failure-case analysis, despite strong SOTA wording in places.
